lead: When every main generator is lost, a small air-driven turbine, the ram air turbine (RAT), drops into the slipstream and powers the emergency buses. A permanent magnet generator (PMG) keeps the engine control alive, and the battery bridges the seconds before the RAT is on line. ETOPS rules set how far, in flying time, a twin may be from a suitable airport, and so how long the remaining sources must keep the essential loads running. Some syllabi cover this only briefly; the APU, the usual third source, is part of the same story.
prereq: You need 3.1 for main sources and 3.3 for battery capacity and usable charge.

blocks.text: Main generators on the engines supply normal power. When all of them fail, the aircraft still needs flight instruments, one radio, the flight controls and engine control. These essential loads sit on the emergency (essential) AC bus and the essential DC bus, which are kept separate from the main buses so a main-bus fault cannot reach them. The changeover runs in a fixed order, automatically. First, protection opens the failed generators' breakers. At the same moment the essential DC bus falls back to the battery through a contactor, so the standby instruments never go dark. Then the RAT deploys and comes up to speed within a few seconds; its generator feeds the emergency AC bus, and an essential TRU (sized for the essential loads only) takes the essential DC bus back from the battery. Each source covers the gap until the next one is ready.

sections.h3: Ram air turbine, PMG and backup converters

blocks.text: Ram air turbine (RAT): a small two-bladed propeller on a strut is released into the airstream. It drives a generator directly, or drives a hydraulic pump whose fluid turns a hydraulic motor and generator; the A320 does it the second way, with an emergency generator of about 5 kVA. Deployment is automatic after loss of all AC power, or manual. The RAT works inside an airspeed band: below it the turbine turns too slowly to carry the load, so the crew keeps speed up; a governor on the blade pitch holds its speed against overspeed. It feeds the emergency AC bus, not the main buses.

Permanent magnet generator (PMG): a magnet rotor spins inside a fixed stator winding. There is no field winding, so its output cannot be switched off by removing field current; only stopping the shaft stops it. On an engine it supplies the electronic engine control (FADEC) with its own power, independent of the aircraft buses; the engine igniters are usually fed from the aircraft AC bus. Its frequency rises with shaft speed, so it is rectified inside the control unit. Backup converters let the battery feed the essential DC bus, and a static inverter makes AC for the AC standby bus from it.

ETOPS means Extended-range Twin-engine Operational Performance Standards. It sets the longest time a twin-engine aircraft may be, at its one-engine-inoperative cruise speed in still air, from a suitable alternate airport. Common approvals are 120 and 180 minutes, with longer ones for some types. The rule is about time, not distance: at 420 kt (knots), 120 minutes is 840 nautical miles (nm) and 180 minutes is 1260 nm. For the electrical system, ETOPS asks whether the remaining sources can carry the essential loads for the whole diversion after a further failure. The battery cannot do this alone; it covers only the gap until the APU generator or the RAT is on line. The time a battery lasts is t = Qusable ÷ I, where t is in hours, Qusable is the usable charge in ampere-hours and I is the current in amperes. Usable charge is less than rated capacity (see aircraft batteries).

sections.h3: The APU as a third source

blocks.text: The auxiliary power unit (APU) is a small gas turbine, usually in the tail cone, that drives its own generator. On the A320 that generator is rated 90 kVA, the same as one engine IDG, so it can replace a lost engine generator completely; on the B787 two APU starter-generators of 225 kVA each do the same job. The APU gives power on the ground before engine start and can be started in flight. On many ETOPS twins the APU generator is the third independent AC source, so ETOPS approval also checks that the APU starts reliably at altitude after a long cold soak, or the APU is run for the whole extended part of the flight. The APU is started from the battery (or, on the B787, from its own lithium-ion APU battery).

examples.question: An aircraft is cleared for ETOPS 120, so it must stay within 120 minutes of a suitable alternate; at 420 kt that is 840 nm. Its essential DC bus draws 2.8 kW at 28 V. The battery is rated 40 Ah and only 50 % may be used. Find the bus current, usable charge and battery time, and say what this means for the diversion.
steps: Bus current I = P / V = 2800 W / 28 V = 100 A.
Time t = Q<sub>usable</sub> / I = 20 Ah / 100 A = 0.2 h.
examples.answer: 100 A, 20 Ah and 12 min; the RAT or APU must take over long before 120 minutes.

traps: Thinking the battery covers the full ETOPS diversion; it only bridges until the RAT or APU generator is online.
Forgetting the RAT airspeed band; below it the turbine cannot carry its load, so the speed must be kept up.
Confusing the PMG with a wound-field generator; no field winding means it cannot be switched off electrically.
Using rated battery Ah instead of usable Ah; only a fraction may be discharged.
Thinking the APU is only for ground use. It can be started in flight and is the third AC source on many ETOPS twins.

quiz.q: What does RAT mean and what turns it?
quiz.a: Ram air turbine; a small propeller in the airstream.

quiz.q: Why can a PMG not be switched off by its field?
quiz.a: It has no field winding; only stopping the shaft stops it.

quiz.q: DC bus 1.4 kW at 28 V; battery 30 Ah, 50 % usable. Find current and time.
Why is the battery not sized for the full ETOPS diversion?
quiz.a: It only bridges until the RAT or APU generator is online; those carry the diversion load.

quiz.q: What happens if the airspeed falls below the RAT's working band, and what does the crew do about it?
quiz.a: The turbine turns too slowly to hold voltage and frequency under load, so the emergency bus voltage sags and loads may drop off. The crew keeps the speed above the RAT minimum and sheds load; below it the battery carries the essential DC bus for a short time only.

quiz.q: Name two jobs the APU generator does on a twin-engine transport.
quiz.a: It supplies AC power on the ground before engine start, and it replaces a failed engine generator in flight (the third AC source on ETOPS flights).

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern RATs often combine a generator and hydraulic pump. Research looks at lightweight PMGs and fault-tolerant emergency buses. Search 'RAT emergency power' and 'ETOPS electrical load analysis'.

figure.caption: The changeover after all generators are lost: the battery holds the essential DC bus for the seconds until the RAT is on line. In the worked example the battery alone would last 12 minutes at 100 A, a tenth of an ETOPS 120 diversion, so it can only bridge.
